concepts.name: Tenth Schedule: Constitutional Basis and Structure
key_dimensions: Added by 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 — not an original provision
Applies to both Houses of Parliament and State Legislatures including Legislative Councils
Does NOT apply to President or Vice-President elections
Distinction between Schedule as a constitutional provision vs. ordinary law — judicial review implications

concepts.name: Merger Exception under Paragraph 4 of Tenth Schedule
key_dimensions: Original Tenth Schedule had TWO exceptions: merger AND split (1/3rd members); split exception was deleted by 91st Amendment Act, 2003
Post-91st Amendment: Only merger of at least 2/3rd of original party members into another party is valid exception
Merger must be of the 'original political party' not just the legislature party — critical distinction
Members who do NOT merge can claim separate group status: this nuance is frequently tested

concepts.name: Deletion of Split Exception by 91st Amendment Act, 2003
key_dimensions: Original Paragraph 3 allowed split if 1/3rd members broke away — deleted entirely in 2003
Rationale: 1/3rd threshold was too easily manipulated, enabling manufactured splits
Post-deletion, no split (however large, below 2/3rd) can save a member from disqualification
UPSC trap: Confusion between old 1/3rd split rule and current 2/3rd merger rule

concepts.name: Speaker/Chairman as Adjudicating Authority: Role and Limitations
key_dimensions: Speaker of Lok Sabha / Chairman of Rajya Sabha decides disqualification petitions — not the Election Commission
Presiding officer's decision is subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan case, 1992)
Conflict of interest issue: Speaker is often a member of the ruling party — reform debates
Kihoto Hollohan: Speaker's decision is NOT final and can be reviewed AFTER a final order, not during pendency

concepts.name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Judicial Review of Anti-Defection
key_dimensions: Supreme Court upheld constitutional validity of Tenth Schedule
Ruled that Paragraph 7 (which barred courts from jurisdiction) was unconstitutional as it required ratification by states (Article 368(2))
Courts CAN intervene but only AFTER the Speaker/Chairman makes a final order — no interim intervention
Established that anti-defection law does not violate freedom of speech or right to vote of legislators

concepts.name: Voluntarily Giving Up Membership of a Political Party
key_dimensions: Paragraph 2(1)(a): Disqualification if a member 'voluntarily gives up membership' of their party
'Voluntary giving up' is WIDER than formal resignation — conduct, public statements, joining rival camps can constitute it (Ravi Naik v. Union of India)
UPSC trap: Formal written resignation is NOT the only trigger — deemed conduct counts
Distinction from voting against party whip (Paragraph 2(1)(b)) — two separate grounds for disqualification

concepts.name: Voting Against Party Whip: Scope and Exceptions
key_dimensions: Paragraph 2(1)(b): Disqualification if member votes contrary to party direction OR abstains from voting in violation of whip
Party can CONDONE such violation within 15 days — if condoned, no disqualification
Whip is issued by the 'political party' — legislature party whip vs. original party whip distinction matters
Three-line whip vs. ordinary whip: Three-line whip makes absence/contrary vote a defection ground

concepts.name: Nominated Members and Anti-Defection Provisions
key_dimensions: Nominated members (e.g., Anglo-Indian in old provision, 12 Rajya Sabha nominees) CAN join a party within 6 months of nomination without attracting disqualification
If they join a party AFTER 6 months, they face disqualification under anti-defection rules
If nominated member joins ANY party AFTER the 6-month window, it triggers Tenth Schedule
UPSC trap: 6-month window applies only to nominated members, NOT to elected members

concepts.name: Speaker as Subject of Disqualification Petition
key_dimensions: If Speaker themselves is alleged to have defected, who decides? — Petition is heard by another member elected by the House
This is a unique procedural asymmetry in the Tenth Schedule framework
Subash Desai v. Principal Secretary case (Maharashtra, 2023) raised questions about Deputy Governor's role when Speaker is under cloud
Reform suggestion: Refer Speaker's disqualification to Election Commission

concepts.name: Anti-Defection and the Office of Speaker: Neutrality Debate
key_dimensions: Constitutional expectation that Speaker acts impartially, but no formal requirement to resign from party
UK convention vs. Indian practice: UK Speaker resigns from party; India has no such binding norm
Supreme Court in Nabam Rebia (2016): Speaker cannot decide disqualification if removal notice is pending against Speaker
Reform proposals: Transfer adjudication to a permanent tribunal or Election Commission

concepts.name: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016): Limits on Speaker's Power
key_dimensions: Supreme Court ruled: Speaker CANNOT hear disqualification petitions when a notice for their own removal is pending
Prevents Speaker from using disqualification power to protect own position
Raised broader question of democratic accountability of the Speaker under anti-defection law
Distinguished from Kihoto Hollohan — procedural fairness dimension added

concepts.name: Anti-Defection and Freedom of Conscience / Dissent
key_dimensions: Tension between Tenth Schedule and Article 105 (freedom of speech of MPs) / Article 194 (MLAs)
Kihoto Hollohan resolved this: Anti-defection restrictions are a REASONABLE restriction on legislative freedom
No exception for voting against party on matters of 'conscience' (unlike some foreign legislatures)
UPSC trap: India has NO conscience vote exception — a common misconception

concepts.name: Disqualification vs. Resignation: Distinct Consequences
key_dimensions: Disqualified member CANNOT contest elections for the remainder of the term from ANY party — this is debated
Supreme Court in Manipur Assembly Speaker case (2020) clarified timelines for deciding disqualification
Disqualified member loses seat; resigned member vacates seat but can re-contest in by-election
Key distinction: Resignation triggers by-election; disqualification may result in being barred from contesting (depending on interpretation)

concepts.name: Time Limit for Deciding Disqualification Petitions
key_dimensions: No statutory time limit prescribed in Tenth Schedule — a major lacuna
Supreme Court has repeatedly directed Speakers to decide within 3 months (Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, 2020)
Delay by Speaker used as political tool — pending petitions allow 'defectors' to continue voting
Law Commission and Election Commission have recommended a fixed time limit (3 months)

concepts.name: Anti-Defection and Independent Members/Small Parties
key_dimensions: An INDEPENDENT member who joins any political party AFTER election faces disqualification
A member elected on a party ticket who later becomes independent is disqualified
Small parties with fewer than 2 members CANNOT form a merger — the 2/3rd rule creates a floor issue
UPSC trap: Independent members have stricter rules — they cannot join any party post-election

concepts.name: Paragraph 2(2): Disqualification of Members Who Abstain
key_dimensions: Abstaining from voting when party whip directs voting is EQUIVALENT to voting against — both are disqualification grounds
This makes the whip legally binding even for abstentions — limits legislative autonomy significantly
Distinction: Absence without leave vs. deliberate abstention — both covered under Paragraph 2(1)(b)
Party can condone within 15 days — the condonation window is the only saving grace

concepts.name: Anti-Defection in Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule applies equally to Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils
Chairman of Rajya Sabha acts as adjudicating authority for RS members
Rajya Sabha members are elected by state legislatures — defection here has indirect democratic implications
Anti-defection in Upper Houses: Less litigated but same legal framework applies

concepts.name: Maharashtra Political Crisis (2022) and Shinde Faction: Merger vs. Faction Test
key_dimensions: Supreme Court (Subash Desai v. Principal Secretary, 2023): Speaker cannot recognize a faction as the 'real party' to avoid disqualification
Court ruled that Speaker's recognition of a rival faction does not automatically save members from disqualification
Election Commission's role in deciding 'real party' symbol vs. Speaker's role in disqualification — two separate tracks
Case highlighted the gap: 2/3rd majority in legislature party does not equal merger under Tenth Schedule if original party does not merge

concepts.name: Election Commission's Role vs. Speaker's Role in Anti-Defection Disputes
key_dimensions: Election Commission decides which faction gets party symbol under Symbols Order, 1968 — separate from disqualification
Speaker decides disqualification under Tenth Schedule — these are PARALLEL proceedings with different outcomes
UPSC trap: Election Commission does NOT decide disqualification; Speaker does NOT decide party symbol
Post-Maharashtra crisis, Supreme Court clarified the two processes are independent and neither binds the other

concepts.name: Proposed Reforms to Anti-Defection Law: Law Commission and Dinesh Goswami Committee
key_dimensions: Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990): Recommended disqualification only for specific votes (no-confidence, budget) — not ALL whip violations
Law Commission (170th Report, 1999): Suggested President/Governor (on EC advice) should decide, not Speaker
Proposal to restrict anti-defection to confidence/money bills to preserve legislative independence
Current consensus: Transfer adjudication to an independent tribunal; fix a 3-month decision deadline
